stances.claim: For years, the prescriptive period for cyberlibel has befuddled magistrates, legislators, lawyers, journalists, and the public. In Tolentino v. People (Aug 6 2018, per J later CJ Teresita Leonardo-de Castro, First Division, via unsigned extended resolution), the Court held the Cybercrime Prevention Act of 2012 -- in relation to RPC Article 90 par. 2 -- prescribes in 15 years; on this basis, the cyberlibel allegedly committed by Wilbert Tolentino had not prescribed.

Five years later, the Court changed its mind. Causing v. People (Oct 11 2023, J Inting, Third Division) applied RPC Article 90 par. 4 and held libel 'shall prescribe in one year.' The Third Division reasoned that cyberlibel and traditional libel are 'one and the same crime' since their elements are the same; ergo, their prescriptive periods should be the same -- i.e., one year. Ironically, though the accused won the battle to fix the prescriptive period to one year, he lost the war because the date of discovery of the allegedly libelous article was not established.

In CJP's Jan 29 2024 column 'Will Maria Ressa, Jinggoy Estrada be acquitted?,' he observed that the First-Third Division conflict should be settled by the full Court, because under the Constitution (Article VIII, Section 4, Item 3) only the Court en banc may modify or reverse a doctrine or principle of law. Fortunately, the separate partial motions for reconsideration filed by the accused and prosecution in Causing v. People were referred to and resolved by the Court en banc via a resolution promulgated on April 8 2026 -- held that cyberlibel prescribes in one year from the 'date of the discovery of the alleged defamatory [online] remarks,' not from publication.

Penned also by J Inting, the resolution -- passed by a hairline 8-7 vote -- clarified that the Tolentino ruling is not a doctrinal or binding precedent since it was contained in an unsigned extended resolution, not in a signed ponencia. Notably, the seven dissenters led by J Antonio T. Kho Jr. argued that traditional libel and cyberlibel are not the same because of 'the qualifying aggravating circumstance of [the] use of ICT'; thus, 'the one-year prescriptive period is no longer controlling, as it is only applicable in traditional libel.'

All told, the matter is now settled: the State's authority to prosecute, and the power of courts to penalize, cyberlibel prescribes in one year, reckoned from the discovery by the offended parties or the authorities of the allegedly defamatory article, not from its publication. The date of discovery must be proven during trial. This ruling, in CJP's humble opinion, balances the rights of journos and the offended parties.

The one-year prescription protects journalists because it mitigates the 'chilling effect' of protracted legal uncertainty. Absent such a limit, every critical cyber publication would expose its author to 15 years of possible criminal prosecution and harassment -- too long for daily grinders such as reporters, columnists, editors, and online podcasters. Since CJP started writing opinions after retiring from the SC almost two decades ago, he has tried to protect journos -- Feb 24 2019 'Is Maria Ressa liable for libel?' explored Ressa-Santos cyberlibel defenses including prescription; June 21 2020 'Cyberlibel and Maria Ressa.' Today, cyberlibel cases filed beyond the one-year prescription reckoned from discovery would result in acquittal.

On the other hand, the 'discovery rule' protects the public. By reckoning the one-year period from discovery rather than publication, the Court acknowledged the unique nature of online libel -- social media like Facebook, LinkedIn, and Instagram have privacy features that limit public exposure. Thus, Vivares v. St. Theresa's College (Sept 29 2014, per J Velasco Jr., Third Division) recognized that social media users can control post-visibility through privacy settings; to presume online posts readily discoverable would be a 'grave legal error.' The discovery rule preserves the public right to seek redress where harm is not readily discoverable.

Speech in cyberspace is not without protection. Neither is it without consequence. Though the law should keep pace with the velocity of digital speech, the Court en banc's ruling is a balanced guardrail in tempering the boundlessness of online expression.

notable_anecdotes: The 'won the battle but lost the war' irony in Causing v. People -- accused succeeded in establishing the one-year prescriptive period but still lost because the date of discovery was not established at trial -- a doctrinal-victory-without-personal-acquittal twist.
The 8-7 hairline en banc vote on April 8 2026 -- among the narrowest doctrinal-margins in recent SC en banc resolutions, capturing the deep judicial division over cyberlibel prescription.

The Tolentino-not-doctrinal-because-unsigned-extended-resolution clarification -- a procedural-doctrinal distinction with major doctrinal-precedence consequences (unsigned-extended-resolution-versus-signed-ponencia hierarchy).

The Kho-dissent ICT-as-qualifying-aggravating-circumstance argument -- sophisticated minority-doctrinal position that cyberlibel is materially distinct from traditional libel, captured for its analytical seriousness even in dissent.

The 'daily grinders such as reporters, columnists, editors, and online podcasters' framing -- CJP including himself implicitly (as a columnist) in the chilling-effect-protectee class, a meta-rhetorical move.
The Vivares v. St. Theresa's College privacy-settings citation -- drawing on a 2014 schoolgirl-Facebook-photo case to ground the discovery-rule doctrine, a creative cross-doctrinal connection.

CJP's self-citation chain -- Feb 24 2019 + June 21 2020 + Jan 29 2024 columns explicitly tracked as part of his journo-protection track record -- among the most concentrated three-column self-citation chains in CJP's corpus.
The 'velocity of digital speech' framing -- captures the law-must-keep-pace pressure on doctrinal evolution in the digital era.
The 'balanced guardrail in tempering the boundlessness of online expression' closing -- CJP's signature both-sides-balance closing-phrase calibrating between freedom and consequence.
The 'Speech in cyberspace is not without protection. Neither is it without consequence' parallel-construction -- CJP's tightest one-sentence balance statement on online-expression rights and limits.
